Long event output for large simulations

TA Trikalinos

2026-08-28

Source: vignettes/Long_output_format.Rmd
Long_output_format.Rmd

What this vignette shows

The vectorized samplers return, by default, a dense matrix of event times: one row per point process, one column per event, with rows that have fewer events than the widest row padded with NA on the right. This is convenient and fast, but the matrix is allocated at the width of the widest row. When event counts vary a lot across point processes – a few heavy processes among many light ones – almost all of that memory holds NA.

The output = "long" option returns the same draw in long format instead: one entry per event, with no padding at all. This vignette shows the format, verifies that the two outputs describe the same realization, and measures the memory and speed differences.

The two formats

A population of 1e+05 processes over (0,4](0, 4], where most processes have a low constant rate (about 1 expected event) and 100 “heavy” processes have rate 10 (about 40 expected events):

rate <- c(rep(0.25, K - 100), rep(10, 100))
lambda_matrix <- matrix(rep(rate, 5), ncol = 5)
time_breaks <- seq(0, 4, length.out = 6)

The dense default:

Z_dense <- vdraw_sc_step(
  lambda_matrix = lambda_matrix,
  time_breaks = time_breaks
)
dim(Z_dense)
#> [1] 100000     54
mean(is.na(Z_dense)) # fraction of the matrix that is padding
#> [1] 0.9809311

The 100 heavy processes set the width of the matrix for everyone, so – as printed above – nearly all cells are NA padding.

The long format, from the same sampler:

Z_long <- vdraw_sc_step(
  lambda_matrix = lambda_matrix,
  time_breaks = time_breaks,
  output = "long"
)
str(Z_long)
#> List of 3
#>  $ id     : int [1:104005] 2 6 6 7 8 8 8 9 11 11 ...
#>  $ time   : num [1:104005] 2.779 2.404 2.481 1.82 0.356 ...
#>  $ n_draws: int 100000

One entry per event: id is the (1-based) index of the point process, ascending, with event times ascending within each id; n_draws records how many processes were sampled. There is no NA anywhere.

How “no events” is represented. A process with zero events contributes no entries – its id is simply absent. n_draws is what distinguishes “process present but with no events” from “process never sampled”:

counts <- tabulate(Z_long$id, nbins = Z_long$n_draws)
sum(counts == 0) # processes with no events: present in n_draws, absent in id
#> [1] 36696

For data.table users the long format is one line from a keyed event table, ready to join against a population table by id:

events <- data.table::data.table(id = Z_long$id, time = Z_long$time)
events[c(1, .N)]
#>        id     time
#>     <int>    <num>
#> 1:      2 2.778843
#> 2: 100000 3.654499

The two outputs describe the same realization

The long format is not a different sampler – the algorithms and their use of the random number stream are identical, and only the recording of events differs. A same-seed pair of draws contains exactly the same event times:

set.seed(1)
Zd <- vdraw_sc_step(
  lambda_matrix = lambda_matrix[1:1000, ], time_breaks = time_breaks
)
set.seed(1)
Zl <- vdraw_sc_step(
  lambda_matrix = lambda_matrix[1:1000, ], time_breaks = time_breaks,
  output = "long"
)
# flatten the dense matrix by row (the long format's grouping) and compare
dense_events <- as.vector(t(Zd))
identical(Zl$time, dense_events[!is.na(dense_events)])
#> [1] TRUE
identical(tabulate(Zl$id, Zl$n_draws), as.integer(rowSums(!is.na(Zd))))
#> [1] TRUE

Memory

The dense matrix costs 8nmax⁡iNi8 \, n \max_i N_i bytes; the long format costs about 12∑iNi12 \sum_i N_i bytes (8 for each time, 4 for each id). The ratio is therefore driven by max⁡iNi/N‾\max_i N_i / \bar N – the heterogeneity of the event counts, not the number of processes. Three populations of 1e+05 processes with the same expected total number of events but increasing heterogeneity:

mem_case <- function(rate_vector, label) {
  lm <- matrix(rep(rate_vector, 5), ncol = 5)
  Zd <- vdraw_sc_step(lambda_matrix = lm, time_breaks = time_breaks)
  Zl <- vdraw_sc_step(lambda_matrix = lm, time_breaks = time_breaks, output = "long")
  data.frame(
    population = label,
    max_events = ncol(Zd),
    dense_MB = round(as.numeric(object.size(Zd)) / 2^20, 1),
    long_MB = round(as.numeric(object.size(Zl)) / 2^20, 1)
  )
}
# equal expected totals (~1.25 e5 events), increasingly concentrated
homogeneous <- rep(0.3125, K)
mild <- c(rep(0.25, K - 5000), rep(1.5, 5000))
extreme <- c(rep(0.25, K - 100), rep(10, 100))
tab <- rbind(
  mem_case(homogeneous, "homogeneous"),
  mem_case(mild, "mildly heterogeneous"),
  mem_case(extreme, "extremely heterogeneous")
)
knitr::kable(tab)
population max_events dense_MB long_MB
homogeneous 8 6.1 1.4
mildly heterogeneous 15 11.4 1.4
extremely heterogeneous 56 42.7 1.2

With homogeneous counts the two formats cost about the same (the dense matrix is narrow, and the long format pays 4 extra bytes per event for the id). As heterogeneity grows, the dense matrix widens with the heaviest row while the long format stays proportional to the actual number of events. In the extreme case the dense matrix is dozens of times larger. The effect scales: at 10710^7 processes the extreme fixture costs gigabytes dense and tens of megabytes long.

Speed

The long format is not a time-memory trade-off – skipping the allocation, NA-filling, and trimming of the wide matrix also saves time:

time_case <- function(rate_vector, label, n_rep = 3) {
  lm <- matrix(rep(rate_vector, 5), ncol = 5)
  td <- system.time(for (i in seq_len(n_rep)) {
    vdraw_sc_step(lambda_matrix = lm, time_breaks = time_breaks)
  })["elapsed"]
  tl <- system.time(for (i in seq_len(n_rep)) {
    vdraw_sc_step(lambda_matrix = lm, time_breaks = time_breaks, output = "long")
  })["elapsed"]
  data.frame(
    population = label,
    dense_ms = round(1000 * td / n_rep),
    long_ms = round(1000 * tl / n_rep)
  )
}
knitr::kable(rbind(
  time_case(homogeneous, "homogeneous"),
  time_case(mild, "mildly heterogeneous"),
  time_case(extreme, "extremely heterogeneous")
))
population dense_ms long_ms
elapsed homogeneous 17 16
elapsed1 mildly heterogeneous 25 16
elapsed2 extremely heterogeneous 70 16

The conditioned samplers work the same way

output = "long" composes with the reporting and generation-conditioning options. For instance, conditioning on at least two events and reporting in long format:

Z <- vdraw_sc_step(
  lambda_matrix = lambda_matrix[1:1000, ],
  time_breaks = time_breaks,
  generate_at_least_K = 2,
  output = "long"
)
min(tabulate(Z$id, Z$n_draws)) # every process has at least 2 events
#> [1] 2

Under a pure upper bound, zero-event processes have positive probability and appear – correctly – as absent ids:

Z <- vdraw_sc_step(
  lambda_matrix = lambda_matrix[1:1000, ],
  time_breaks = time_breaks,
  generate_at_most_K = 1,
  output = "long"
)
table(tabulate(Z$id, Z$n_draws))
#> 
#>   0   1 
#> 480 520

vdraw_cumulative_intensity() also accepts output = "long"; on its conditioned (order-statistics) path the long result is built without any dense intermediate, and Lambda_inv is evaluated once on the event vector.

Which format to use

  • Dense (default): first-event workloads (report_first_K = 1), homogeneous event counts, or any code that expects the matrix layout. Nothing changes for existing code.
  • Long: many processes with ragged event counts – event-history simulations, heavy-tailed intensities, or whenever the events feed a data.table/long-format pipeline anyway. Memory is proportional to the events actually drawn, and the draw is somewhat faster.
